contests.title: Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance.
contests.fiscal: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
contests.yes_means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
contests.no_means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.

official_args.for: Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers—teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
official_args.against: NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED.

contests.listed_supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 1

contests.title: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
contests.fiscal: State budget reserves would be higher.
contests.yes_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
contests.no_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.

official_args.for: Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
official_args.against: Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

contests.listed_supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 2

contests.title: Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education.
contests.fiscal: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.
contests.yes_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
contests.no_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.

official_args.for: PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
official_args.against: Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

contests.listed_supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
contests.listed_opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 3

contests.title: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
contests.fiscal: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.
contests.yes_means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
contests.no_means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.

official_args.for: YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
official_args.against: Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

contests.listed_supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog
contests.listed_opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 4

contests.title: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.
contests.fiscal: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled.
contests.yes_means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
contests.no_means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.

official_args.for: Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
official_args.against: Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 5

contests.title: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State.
contests.fiscal: No direct state or local costs.
contests.yes_means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
contests.no_means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.

official_args.for: Zero Taxpayer Cost—No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
official_args.against: NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

contests.listed_supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 37

contests.title: Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants.
contests.fiscal: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue.
contests.yes_means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
contests.no_means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.

official_args.for: YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38! www.YESon38.com
official_args.against: California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

contests.listed_supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 38

contests.title: Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification.
contests.fiscal: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements.
contests.yes_means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
contests.no_means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

official_args.for: Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
official_args.against: No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.

contests.listed_supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn
contests.listed_opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 39

contests.title: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit.
contests.fiscal: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires.
contests.yes_means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
contests.no_means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

official_args.for: Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
official_args.against: Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

contests.listed_supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
contests.listed_opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 40

contests.title: Prohibits New State Taxes that Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes.
contests.fiscal: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.
contests.yes_means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
contests.no_means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

official_args.for: Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
official_args.against: Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

contests.listed_supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
contests.listed_opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 41

contests.title: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure.
contests.fiscal: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
contests.yes_means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
contests.no_means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

official_args.for: California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
official_args.against: This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

contests.listed_supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA
contests.listed_opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 42

contests.title: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
contests.fiscal: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
contests.yes_means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
contests.no_means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

official_args.for: Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
official_args.against: PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

contests.listed_supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
contests.listed_opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 43

contests.title: Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services.
contests.fiscal: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees.
contests.yes_means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
contests.no_means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.

official_args.for: Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
official_args.against: Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

contests.listed_opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 44

contests.title: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals.
contests.fiscal: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects.
contests.yes_means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
contests.no_means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.

official_args.for: The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
official_args.against: PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

contests.listed_supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing
contests.listed_opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 45

contests.title: Regional Transit Measure
contests.question: To prevent major service cuts to BART and other transit, avoid increased traffic, and reduce pollution by: Preserving BART, Caltrain, VTA, SamTrans, AC Transit, Muni, other transit for everyone, including workers, students, seniors, persons with disabilities; Supporting transit safety, cleanliness, affordability, reliability; Repairing targeted roads/potholes; Requiring financial transparency, oversight, accountability; shall the measure enacting a 0.5% (Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara counties), and 1% (San Francisco) sales tax for 14 years generating approximately $980,000,000 annually, be adopted?
contests.threshold: 50%+1 of all votes cast in the five Bay Area counties
contests.proposal: This measure was placed on the ballot by voter initiative, signed by the requisite number of voters within the Public Transit Revenue Measure District (“District”). The District was created by the Legislature through Senate Bill 63 (“SB 63”) in 2025 (Government Code sections 67700-67788), which was enacted to preserve and improve public transit service in the San Francisco Bay Area. The District comprises the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara, and the City and County of San Francisco, and is governed by the same board that governs the Metropolitan Transportation Commission (“MTC”). SB 63 authorizes District voters to approve a retail transactions and use tax (commonly referred to as a sales tax) for specified purposes. This measure would impose a tax of 0.5% in the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara and 1.0% in the City and County of San Francisco. The tax would be imposed and collected in largely the same manner as a state-imposed sales tax. The tax would be in effect for 14 years and would not count toward the statutory limit on combined local sales tax rates. It is estimated that the tax would raise approximately $980 million per year. After payment of defined costs, including election costs and administrative expenses, the District must transfer all remaining revenues to MTC and county transportation agencies for distribution and expenditure according to percentages set forth in the measure, which vary by county and recipient. Recipients include BART, Muni, Caltrain, AC Transit, Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority, San Francisco Bay Ferry, Golden Gate Transit, smaller bus operators in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, and county transportation agencies. Revenues would also support free and reduced-cost transit transfers, expansion of the Clipper START reduced-fare program, accessibility programs, mapping and wayfinding and transit priority projects and programs, and repavement projects for roads served by fixed-route transit. While the tax would be imposed throughout the District, the allocation of revenue generated in each county, and the authorized uses of those funds, would vary. For example, 64.70% of all revenues generated in Alameda County would be allocated to BART for transit operations expenses. By contrast, 84.37% of all revenues generated in Santa Clara County would be allocated to the Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority for public transit expenses and roadway repavement projects on roads served by fixed-route transit. Such repavement projects would be an authorized use of measure revenues in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, but would not be authorized in the City and County of San Francisco. Revenue allocation is set forth in Section 12 of the measure. Tax revenues would be subject to accountability requirements in SB 63, which requires BART, Muni, AC Transit, and Caltrain to undergo financial efficiency reviews and adopt implementation plans and authorizes MTC to withhold funds from any of those operators for noncompliance. The measure would also require an independent oversight committee to review whether all revenues are distributed as required. The tax would become effective if approved by a majority of those voting on the measure throughout the entire District.
contests.yes_means: a vote to impose the tax described above for 14 years.
contests.no_means: a vote against imposing the tax.
contests.how_placed: On May 26, 2026, the “Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative” was submitted to election officials in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, as well as the City and County of San Francisco. The petition included 306,288 unverified signatures. State law required 187,119 valid signatures to qualify the initiative for the ballot. This number is equal to 5% of the total number of registered voters within the District. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition showed that an estimated 235,503 signatures were valid. Because this number was greater than the 205,831 signature threshold, which represents 110% of the required number of signatures, the petition was found to be sufficient. On July 1, 2026, the District Elections Official certified that the petition contained enough valid signatures to qualify for the November 3, 2026 ballot.

contests.title: Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions
contests.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to align it with how some City departments currently operate, change some processes, eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies, and require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes?
contests.way_it_is_now: The Charter is the City’s constitution and establishes the organization, powers, and responsibilities for many City departments. The Charter and other voter-approved laws also create many City commissions and advisory bodies and describe their powers, duties, membership and removal rules, and reporting requirements. Over time, some of these laws have become obsolete. The Charter and most laws passed by the voters can only be changed with voter approval.
contests.proposal:
Proposition A would align the Charter with how some City departments currently operate, change some processes, and eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies. Proposition A would require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes. Proposition A would:
• change the language of the Charter to reflect how some City departments currently operate in order to clarify responsibilities and update rules, procedures, and reporting requirements.
• change some processes. For example: allowing legal settlements to be approved by resolution instead of by ordinance.
• require a task force to meet every ten years to recommend changes to commissions.
• eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies by, for example: eliminating some commissions and advisory bodies, combining and renaming some advisory bodies, and moving some commissions and advisory bodies from the Charter into the Municipal Code.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to amend the Charter to align it with how some City departments currently operate, change some processes, eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies, and require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
contests.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a moderate impact on the cost of government, saving $365,000 to $450,000 annually.

contests.title: Establishing a Municipal Finance Corporation and a Public Bank
contests.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation and a public bank?
contests.way_it_is_now: A municipal finance corporation (MFC) is a government-owned non-profit corporation that makes loans but does not take deposits. A public bank is a government-owned non-profit corporation that both makes loans and takes deposits. There is no local law authorizing the City to create a municipal finance corporation or a public bank.
contests.proposal:
Proposition B would amend the City Charter to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation if the City has sufficient funding and resources. After three years of operation, the municipal finance corporation may become a public bank. The MFC would make loans but would not take deposits. If the MFC becomes a public bank, the public bank would make loans and also take deposits. The MFC and public bank would provide services to support:
• affordable housing development,
• affordable homeownership,
• small business development,
• environmental sustainability, and
• environmental justice. These services would be available to individual City residents and to projects and businesses located in the City. Under Proposition B, the MFC and public bank would each be governed by a board of directors. Each board would be appointed and overseen by its own oversight commission. The members of each oversight commission would be appointed by the Board of Supervisors, Mayor, Treasurer-Tax Collector, Controller, and City Attorney.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation and a public bank.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation and a public bank.
contests.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would not directly impact the cost of government as the Charter amendment does not require the City to create a Municipal Finance Corporation (MFC) that could transition into a Public Bank.

contests.title: Changes to Ballot Measure Process
contests.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters in San Francisco (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for calling special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn before an election, and remove the ability of a minority of Board of Supervisors members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot?
contests.proposal:
Proposition D would amend the Charter to increase the requirements to put measures on the ballot by:
• Increasing the number of signatures required to place a signature initiative on the ballot from 2% to 8% (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) of the registered voters in San Francisco.
• Increasing the number of signatures required to call a special election on an ordinance from 10% of the votes cast for Mayor in the last election to 10% of the registered voters in San Francisco. Currently, this is about 53,100 signatures. Proposition D would allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn up to 102 days before the election. Proposition D would also change the requirements to put measures on the ballot by:
• Removing the ability of four or more Board members to place a measure on the ballot without a Board vote;
• Removing the ability of the Mayor to independently place a measure on the ballot; The Board could still place measures on the ballot by a majority vote.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn, and remove the ability of a minority of Board members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.

contests.title: City Administrator’s Authority and Changes to City Contracting
contests.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to give the City Administrator more authority by centralizing the City’s purchasing rules and processes, changing how the City approves purchasing rules, changing when contracts and leases require Board of Supervisors approval, and extending the City Administrator’s term?
contests.way_it_is_now:
The City Administrator’s Office is responsible for most of the City’s purchasing. However, authority for the City’s purchasing and technology is shared among the City Administrator’s Office, the Board of Supervisors, the Mayor, and some City departments.
• Rules Regulating Purchasing: The Board of Supervisors (Board) may adopt ordinances that set the rules about how the City selects contractors and enters into contracts for goods, services, construction, and grants (referred to below as Purchasing).
• Board Approval of Various Agreements: With some exceptions, the City’s Charter requires the Board to approve:
• Contracts and leases that bring in $1,000,000 or more in revenue to the City, and
• Contracts that cost the City $10,000,000 or more. The Board must also approve certain amendments to these agreements.
• City Administrator’s Term: The Mayor appoints the City Administrator to a five-year term, subject to Board approval.
• City Administrator’s Authority: The City Administrator sets Purchasing rules and processes governing goods and services except for some goods and services of the Municipal Transportation Agency, Public Utilities Commission, Port Commission, and some arts departments. The City Administrator also oversees technology policies and manages disposal of City personal property for most departments.
contests.proposal:
Proposition E would:
• Rules Regulating Purchasing: Give the City Administrator exclusive authority to propose ordinances that change how the City selects contractors and enters into contracts for goods, services, construction, and grants (Purchasing). The Board and Mayor may not amend the ordinances, but they can:
• Approve or reject the ordinances within 60 days, or
• If no action is taken within 60 days, the ordinances would be approved. Proposition E does not change the current Board authority for Purchasing ordinances that mainly address wages, workplace health and safety, utilization of local business, or labor agreements.
• Board Approval of Various Agreements: Increase the dollar amount requiring Board approval to:
• Contracts and leases that bring in $4,500,000 or more in revenue to the City,
• Contracts that cost the City $25,000,000 or more. Starting in 2032, the City’s Controller would adjust these dollar amounts every five years for inflation. Proposition E would require Board approval for major amendments to these agreements.
• City Administrator’s Term: Increase the City Administrator’s term from five to ten years.
• City Administrator’s Authority: The City Administrator would set Purchasing rules and processes for all goods, services, construction, and grants that all City departments must follow, except as limited by other laws. Most departments would now be subject to the City Administrator’s authority regarding technology policies and the disposal of City personal property. These rules would override those departments’ conflicting rules and policies.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to give the City Administrator more authority by centralizing the City’s Purchasing rules and processes, changing how the City approves Purchasing rules, changing when contracts and leases require Board approval, and extending the City Administrator’s term.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
contests.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact on the cost of government, although at a level that cannot be determined at this time.
contests.how_placed: On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition E to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot. 53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

contests.title: Changes to Executive Branch Management
contests.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer responsibilities between departments, hire deputy mayors, and hire some and fire most department heads; and to allow City officials to remove members of boards and commissions without cause?
contests.way_it_is_now:
The Mayor is the chief executive officer of the City. The Mayor directly supervises nearly 50 City departments, which are established by Charter or ordinance. Most City departments are established by Charter.
• Transfer of Functions: The Mayor can transfer responsibilities between departments established by ordinance, as long as the Board of Supervisors (Board) does not object. The Mayor cannot transfer responsibilities for departments established by the Charter.
• Deputy Mayors: The Mayor cannot hire deputy mayors to supervise most departments established by the Charter.
• Department Heads: In most cases, the Mayor must select a department head from candidates recommended by the board or commission that oversees that department. Usually, the board or commission can fire the department head, but the Mayor cannot.
• Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board and other officials appoint members to City boards and commissions. Appointed members can usually only be suspended or removed if the member engaged in official misconduct or committed certain felonies.
contests.proposal:
Proposition F would amend the Charter to allow the Mayor to do the following:
• Transfer of Functions: Transfer responsibilities between most departments or combine departments under a single department head, regardless of whether the Department was established by ordinance or Charter and as long as the Board does not object. The Mayor cannot eliminate any responsibilities established by Charter. The Mayor could also assign the oversight of these transferred responsibilities to that department’s commission. The Mayor cannot transfer responsibilities of these departments:
• City Administrator, Controller, Board of Appeals, Port, Airport, Asian Art Museum, Fine Arts Museums, San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, Public Utilities Commission, Civil Service Commission, Department of Human Resources, Retirement Board, Health Service System, Department of Elections, Ethics Commission, or departments headed by other elected officials. The responsibilities of the Department of Police Accountability cannot be transferred to the Police Department, and the responsibilities of the Sheriff’s Inspector General cannot be transferred to the Sheriff.
• Deputy Mayors: Hire deputy mayors to supervise most departments established by the Charter.
• Department Heads: Hire some and fire most department heads without board or commission involvement. The Mayor cannot hire or fire certain department heads that are exempt (see List of Exemptions in Words You Need To Know).
• Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board and other officials who appoint board and commission members could remove them at any time without cause. This does not apply to the Board of Appeals, Civil Service Commission, or Ethics Commission. The Mayor cannot eliminate any board or commission established by the Charter.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer responsibilities, hire deputy mayors, hire some and fire most department heads, and allow City officials to remove members of boards or commissions without cause.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
contests.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact on the cost of government, although at a level that cannot be determined at this time.

This number is equal to 10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

contests.title: Parcel Tax to Fund Muni Operations
contests.question: Shall the City fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate at rates ranging from $129 per parcel up to a maximum of $400,000 per parcel, depending on the type of property and its size and adjusted annually for inflation, for estimated revenue of $177 million a year for 15 years?
contests.way_it_is_now: The Municipal Railway (Muni) provides public transit in San Francisco, including bus, light rail, streetcar, and cable car. Muni provides over 500,000 rides per weekday. Muni service is funded by transit fares and local, state and federal sources, but not through a parcel tax. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, that the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years. Owners of rent-controlled residential property in the City are generally limited in what costs they can pass onto their tenants.
contests.proposal:
Starting July 1, 2027, and continuing until June 30, 2042, Proposition H would fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate in San Francisco. The tax would be adjusted annually for inflation. The proposed 2027 tax rates would be:
• Single-Family Residential Parcels:
• A base tax of $129.
• For buildings with more than 3,000 square feet of building area:
• $0.42 per square foot between 3,001 and 5,000, and
• $1.99 per square foot over 5,000.
• Multifamily Residential Parcels:
• A base tax of $249.
• For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area:
• $0.195 per square foot over 5,000.
• This tax is capped at $50,000 per parcel.
• Non-Residential Parcels:
• A base tax of $799.
• For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area:
• $0.76 per square foot between 5,001 and 50,000,
• $0.84 per square foot between 50,001 and 250,000, and
• $0.99 per square foot over 250,000.
• This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel.
• Mixed-Use Parcels:
• A base tax of $799.
• For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area:
• A combination of the marginal rates for residential and non-residential parcels above.
• This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel.
• Parcels with No Buildings:
• No base tax.
• $392 for land area over 2,000 square feet. The tax would not apply to: 1. Properties or portions of properties not required to pay standard property taxes; and 2. Single Room Occupancy (SRO) units and their shared facilities such as kitchens or bathrooms. Most homeowners aged 65 or older living in their primary home would get a discount or pay no tax. Revenues from the tax would only be used for Muni service and administering the tax. In addition to the annual required audit by an independent auditor, an annual report and efficiency review would be required. This measure would increase the City’s spending limit for four years. Owners could pass up to 50% of the tax onto tenants in rent-controlled units where the rent was set before June 1, 2027, up to a maximum of $65 per unit per year.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want the City to fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
contests.fiscal: Should the proposed parcel tax be approved by the voters, in my opinion, based on currently available parcel data it would generate approximately $177 million annually for Muni transit service starting in Fiscal Year (FY) 2027-2028, and would increase over time as the per parcel taxes are adjusted for inflation each year.

This number is equal to 2% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

contests.title: Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax
contests.question: Shall the City permanently dedicate half of the transfer tax revenues collected when certain real estate with a value or sales price of more than $10,000,000 changes hands, which will continue to be taxed at rates of 5.5% to 6%, to be spent only on affordable housing, including social housing developments and housing assistance, and exempt certain sales from the dedicated portion of the tax, for an estimated annual revenue decrease of approximately $1 million?
contests.way_it_is_now:
The City collects a transfer tax when most real estate changes hands. The tax rates depend on the property’s sales price or value and the two highest tax rates are:
• 5.5% for properties between $10,000,000 and under $25,000,000, and
• 6% for properties at $25,000,000 or more. Some real estate transfers are exempt from the tax or are subject to reduced rates.
• Reduce the transfer tax from 6% to 3%
• Impose a new transfer tax of 3% This measure will not increase the tax rate on the transfer of any property above what is charged today. The same exemptions and tax reductions from the current transfer tax would still apply to the new transfer tax. The new transfer tax would also exempt the first sale of certain multifamily real estate if it is sold within 5 years of completion of new residential units. Tax Revenue Spending Revenues generated from the transfer tax may be spent for any governmental purpose. The City could spend revenue from the new transfer tax only on: The Board of Supervisors (Board) may amend, reduce, suspend, or repeal the transfer tax without voter approval. Voters must approve any increase of the transfer tax. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years.
contests.proposal:
Proposition I would dedicate half of the transfer tax revenues when certain real estate with a value or sales price of more than $10,000,000 changes hands, to be spent only on affordable housing, including social housing developments and housing assistance. Specifically, the measure would: Transfer Tax For properties with a sales price or value between $10,000,000 and under $25,000,000:
• Reduce the current transfer tax from 5.5% to 2.75%
• Impose a new transfer tax of 2.75% For properties with a sales price or value at $25,000,000 or more:
• At least 60% for affordable housing production, with at least half to social housing developments;
• At least 25% towards the acquisition or rehabilitation of affordable housing, with at least 60% to acquisition of existing housing units; and
• At least 10% to tenant stabilization/homeless prevention programs, with at least half to eviction defense and prevention; The Board could only change the transfer tax consistent with the purpose of the tax. All other changes would require voter approval. Proposition I would approve an unlimited number of new affordable housing units for low-income households funded by revenue from the new transfer tax. Proposition I would require the City to submit annual reports to the Board and Mayor on the use of the new tax revenue. Proposition I would increase the City’s spending limit for four years.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to dedicate half of the transfer tax revenues when certain real estate with a value or sales price of more than $10,000,000 changes hands, to be spent only on affordable housing, including social housing developments and housing assistance.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
contests.fiscal: Should the proposed ordinance be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would represent a moderate annual decrease of approximately $1 million to the City’s overall revenues starting in Fiscal Year (FY) 2027-28.

This number is equal to 2% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

contests.title: Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax
contests.question: Shall the City permanently apply a transfer tax of between 0.5% and 6% of a property’s fair market value, on the transfer of properties such as commercial, industrial, and large residential properties, that are transferred to a lender because of foreclosure or to avoid foreclosure, for estimated annual revenue of $100 million to $150 million?
contests.way_it_is_now: San Francisco charges a tax when most real estate property in the City changes hands. The amount of the tax depends on the property’s sales price or value. When a lender takes over a property through foreclosure, or when an owner hands over a property to the lender to avoid foreclosure, there is a tax break. The lender pays tax only on the difference between what the property sold for and what is still owed to the lender, including interest and foreclosure costs. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years.
contests.proposal: Proposition J would apply a transfer tax for properties such as commercial, industrial, and large residential real estate that a lender takes through foreclosure or is handed over to the lender to avoid foreclosure. Starting March 1, 2027, these properties would be taxed on their full market value. The tax break would still apply to the transfer of: 1. single-family residences, 2. multi-family residential buildings with fewer than five units, and 3. mixed-use properties with fewer than five residential units and only one floor of non-residential space. Proposition J would increase the City’s spending limit for four years.
contests.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to apply a transfer tax for properties such as commercial, industrial, and large residential properties, that are transferred to a lender because of foreclosure.
contests.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
contests.fiscal: Should the proposed initiative ordinance be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would significantly increase the City’s Real Property Transfer Tax revenues although the amount generated each year would be unpredictable and likely to change significantly year-to-year.
